purpose: Shorter pupil sentences and concrete actions; all investigation phases, access routes, subject vocabulary, model limits and printed teaching retained. Mark the genuine adult source bibliography using the established addressee attribute.

changes.from: First retrieve the previous lesson; the workshop includes its own check and tidy-up.
changes.to: First recall the last lesson. This workshop has time to check and tidy up.

changes.from: Use the phases below. Choose a supported, standard or stretch route with your adult; pointing, signing, directing, drawing or writing can show the same science.
changes.to: Follow the steps below. Choose a route with your adult. You can point, sign, draw or write. You can tell an adult what to do. Each way can show your science.

changes.from: First revisit the eight-card sort with an adult. Then investigate fish and beetle using the supplied body evidence: point to the support, choose BACKBONE / NO BACKBONE, and make one two-clue card by pointing or dictating.
changes.to: Sort the eight cards again with an adult. Look at the fish and beetle body clues. Point to what holds each body up. Choose BACKBONE or NO BACKBONE. Make a card with two clues. You can point or ask an adult to write.

changes.from: Revisit your eight-card sort. Investigate all four evidence cases, justify one decision, then make a two-clue card whose answer depends on body structure, not size or legs.
changes.to: Sort your eight cards again. Read or hear all four body clues. Give a reason for one choice. Then make a card with two clues. Use what is inside the body. Size or the number of legs will not tell us if it has a backbone.

changes.from: Investigate all four cases. Make a two-clue mystery card and test it with an adult or chosen partner. Explain why a hard outer case or visible body segments are not evidence of a backbone.
changes.to: Check all four cases. Make a card with two clues and hide the name. Ask an adult or a partner to solve it. A hard outer case is not a backbone. Rings on a body are not proof of one either. Use the body clues to say why.

changes.from: Return to Monday’s sort. Say, point or show the rule; choose a reader, pointer or card-mover role.
changes.to: Look at Monday’s sort. Say, point to or show the rule. Choose to read, point or move cards.

changes.from: Use the body evidence cards below. First cover the evidence column and predict. Reveal it, classify each case, then make a two-clue card for one animal from the first lesson.
changes.to: Use the body clues below. First hide the clues. Predict each group. Show the clues and sort each case. Then choose one animal from the first lesson. Make two clues for it. Keep its name hidden.

changes.from: Ask an adult or chosen partner to check one decision against the backbone rule. Quiet self-check with the evidence column also counts.
changes.to: Ask an adult or a partner to check one choice. Does it fit the backbone rule? You can also check on your own. Use the body clues.

changes.from: Keep or correct one decision and show the reason. Save the card and mat together; return the materials.
changes.to: Keep or change one choice. Show why. Save your card with the mat. Put the kit back.

changes.from: Printed evidence cards, first-period mat, pencil or movable labels. Adults can read and cut; pupils can point. No live animals, handling of bodies or touching spines.
changes.to: Use the printed cards, your first mat, a pencil or loose labels. An adult can read and cut. You can point. Use only the paper models. Do not touch an animal or anyone’s spine.

changes.from: An internal skeleton includes a backbone.
changes.to: Bones inside the body include a backbone.

changes.from: Bones inside the body include a backbone, even though it has wings.
changes.to: It has wings. It also has bones inside its body, with a backbone.

changes.from: A hard outer case supports the body; it has no backbone.
changes.to: A hard outer case holds the body up. There is no backbone inside.

changes.from: Muscles act against fluid inside the body; its outer rings are not bones.
changes.to: Muscles push against fluid inside the body. The rings on its skin are not bones.

changes.from: First retrieve the previous lesson; the workshop includes its own check and tidy-up.
changes.to: First recall the last lesson. This workshop has time to check and tidy up.

changes.from: Use the phases below. Choose a supported, standard or stretch route with your adult; pointing, signing, directing, drawing or writing can show the same science.
changes.to: Follow the steps below. Choose a route with your adult. You can point, sign, draw or write. You can tell an adult what to do. Each way can show your science.

changes.from: Use a prepared card arm or direct an adult. Move CONTRACTS / RELAXES labels for bending, then for straightening. Show which part pulls each time.
changes.to: Use a card arm made by an adult. You can ask the adult to move it for you. Bend it, then make it straight. Move the CONTRACTS and RELAXES labels. Show which part pulls each time.

changes.from: Build the arm, test bending and straightening, and explain the biceps/triceps labels in one response. Correct a label after checking the diagram.
changes.to: Build the arm. Test a bend. Then make it straight. Use the biceps and triceps labels to say what happens. Check the diagram. Fix a label if you need to.

changes.from: Build and test both actions. Explain why pulling partners are needed, and state one difference between the string model and real contracting muscle.
changes.to: Build and test both moves. Say why it needs a pull on each side. The string stands for a muscle. What is one way the string is not like a real muscle?

changes.from: Recover Monday’s two labels. Check that the elbow join turns and choose a model-maker or director role.
changes.to: Find Monday’s two labels. Check that the elbow join can turn. Choose to make the model or tell an adult how to make it.

changes.from: Build or direct an adult to build the card arm. Test a gentle bend and straighten. Move CONTRACTS / RELAXES labels for each action; compare the string model with the lesson diagram.
changes.to: Build the card arm or tell an adult how to build it. Pull gently to bend it. Try the other string to make it straight. Move the CONTRACTS and RELAXES labels for each move. Check the model against the lesson diagram.

changes.from: Use the diagram to check whether both directions have a pulling partner. An adult can move the model while you direct.
changes.to: Check the diagram. Is there a string to pull for each move? You can tell an adult how to move the model.

changes.from: Fix one label or connection, show both actions again, record one limitation of the model if ready, and clear the bench.
changes.to: Fix one label or join. Show both moves again. If ready, note one way the model differs from a real arm. Clear the bench.

changes.from: Two card strips, one adult-fitted split pin, two loose strings and labels. Adults prepare holes and cuts. Use gentle pulls, keep pins secured and use no stretched elastic. No one has to move or show their own arm.
changes.to: Use two card strips, two loose strings and labels. An adult cuts the card, makes the holes and fits the split pin. Keep the pin fixed in place. Pull gently. Do not use stretched elastic. No one has to move or show their own arm.

changes.from: First retrieve the previous lesson; the workshop includes its own check and tidy-up.
changes.to: First recall the last lesson. This workshop has time to check and tidy up.

changes.from: Use the phases below. Choose a supported, standard or stretch route with your adult; pointing, signing, directing, drawing or writing can show the same science.
changes.to: Follow the steps below. Choose a route with your adult. You can point, sign, draw or write. You can tell an adult what to do. Each way can show your science.

changes.from: Revisit the six food cards. With an adult reading the table, choose examples for energy and for growth/repair. Point to a reason, then change one choice when a case changes.
changes.to: Look at the six food cards again. Ask an adult to read the table. Choose a food for energy and one for growth and repair. Point to a reason. When the case changes, change one choice.

changes.from: Use the table to make two different model selections. Explain two contributions and revise one selection for the changed case. You may talk, sign, draw or write.
changes.to: Use the table to make two sets of food cards. Say what two of the foods give the body. Change one set to fit the new case. You can talk, sign, draw or write.

changes.from: Compare two possible selections for the same case. Explain why no single example guarantees every nutrient, and why a food can contribute to more than one body job.
changes.to: Make two sets that fit the same case. What is the same? What differs? Why can one food help with more than one body job? Why should we not expect one food to give every nutrient?

changes.from: Recover Monday’s food-job choices. Use example menus only; nobody needs to describe food at home.
changes.to: Find Monday’s food-job choices. Use the made-up menus. No one needs to tell us what they eat at home.

changes.from: Use the information cards to build a model choice for two different cases. Explain what each choice contributes, then change the case and revise one choice. A food may contribute to more than one job.
changes.to: Read or hear the food cards. Make a set for each of the two cases. Say what each food gives the body. Change the case. Change one food choice to fit it. A food may help with more than one job.

changes.from: Check one explanation with the information table or an adult. Does it say what the food provides, rather than only whether somebody likes it?
changes.to: Check one reason with the table or an adult. Does it say what the food gives the body? “I like it” does not tell us that.

changes.from: Improve one choice or explanation. Keep a before/after record and return the cards.
changes.to: Make one choice or reason clearer. Keep a note of it before and after the change. Put the cards back.

changes.from: Paper food cards and the supplied information table only. No tasting or real food; no discussion of weight, calories or pupils’ personal diets. This is a simplified classroom model, not an individual meal plan.
changes.to: Use only the paper food cards and table. There is no real food to taste. Do not discuss weight, calories or what pupils eat. This model helps us learn about food jobs. It is not a meal plan for a real person.

changes.from: Water is an additional information card.
changes.to: There is also a water card.

changes.from: Starchy carbohydrate supplies energy.
changes.to: Starchy carbohydrate gives us energy.

changes.from: Protein supports growth and repair; they also provide carbohydrate and fibre.
changes.to: Protein helps us grow and repair the body. These foods also give us carbohydrate and fibre.

changes.from: Different examples provide vitamins, minerals and fibre.
changes.to: These foods give us vitamins, minerals and fibre. The amounts differ from food to food.

changes.from: Helps transport substances and regulate temperature; it does not supply food energy.
changes.to: Helps carry things around the body. It helps keep the body at the right heat. It does not give us food energy.

changes.from: Keep those examples; add choices that give a wider range of nutrients.
changes.to: Keep those cards. Add foods that give a wider range of nutrients.

changes.from: Make a meat-free version using the information cards; explain what replaces the protein contribution.
changes.to: Use the cards to make a meat-free menu. Which food takes the place of meat as a source of protein?

changes.from: First retrieve the previous lesson; the workshop includes its own check and tidy-up.
changes.to: First recall the last lesson. This workshop has time to check and tidy up.

changes.from: Use the phases below. Choose a supported, standard or stretch route with your adult; pointing, signing, directing, drawing or writing can show the same science.
changes.to: Follow the steps below. Choose a route with your adult. You can point, sign, draw or write. You can tell an adult what to do. Each way can show your science.

changes.from: Place or point to the eight food examples. With an adult, compare the two cases and choose a meat-free protein swap. Show which group the replacement belongs to.
changes.to: Place or point to the eight food cards. Look at both cases with an adult. Choose a food with protein to use in place of meat. Show its food group.

changes.from: Build and label a model plate. Compare both cases, make the meat-free swap, and explain why the replacement serves a similar food-group role.
changes.to: Build and label a model plate. Look at both cases. Swap the meat for a food with protein. Say why the new food fits the same broad group.

changes.from: Compare two possible meat-free swaps. Explain why balance concerns food over a day or week, why a single plate is a model, and one fact it cannot tell us about a person’s needs.
changes.to: Find two foods with protein that could take the place of meat. How do they compare? Balance is about what we eat over a day or week. Say why one model plate cannot show all a person’s food needs.

changes.from: Return to Monday’s plate mat. Choose card-moving, drawing or directing an adult; recall the food groups.
changes.to: Find Monday’s plate mat. Name or point to the food groups. Choose to move cards, draw or tell an adult where to place them.

changes.from: Build a model selection using the supplied examples. Compare it with the second case, make a meat-free version, then explain a swap that keeps the same broad food-group contribution.
changes.to: Build a model plate with the cards. Look at the second case. What is the same? What differs? Make a meat-free plate. Say why your swap still gives us food from the same broad group.

changes.from: Check the group labels with an adult or the information cards. Ask whether a missing group is missing from this model or simply provided elsewhere in the day.
changes.to: Check the group labels with an adult or the food cards. Is a group missing from this model? Could food from that group be eaten at another time in the day?

changes.from: Revise one model and record why. Put both versions side by side, save one explanation and reset materials.
changes.to: Change one model and show why. Put the old and new sets side by side. Save one reason for the change. Put the kit back.

changes.from: Paper plate mats, group labels and example cards only. No real food, taste test, portion measurement or judgement about anybody’s eating. Keep any individual dietary requirements with the pupil’s existing support plan.
changes.to: Use only paper mats, group labels and food cards. There is no real food or taste test. Do not measure portions or judge what anyone eats. An adult follows each pupil’s support plan for their own food needs.

changes.from: Which examples could replace chicken while retaining a protein source?
changes.to: Which cards could take the place of chicken and still give us protein?

changes.from: How are the groups similar even though the foods differ?
changes.to: The foods differ. How are their food groups alike?

changes.from: These cards show food groups, not exact portions. Variety and balance are considered over a day or week; every meal need not copy a diagram.
changes.to: These cards show food groups. They do not show exact portions. Look for a range of foods and balance over a day or week. Each meal does not have to copy a diagram.

changes.from: First retrieve the previous lesson; the workshop includes its own check and tidy-up.
changes.to: First recall the last lesson. This workshop has time to check and tidy up.

changes.from: Use the phases below. Choose a supported, standard or stretch route with your adult; pointing, signing, directing, drawing or writing can show the same science.
changes.to: Follow the steps below. Choose a route with your adult. You can point, sign, draw or write. You can tell an adult what to do. Each way can show your science.

changes.from: Order grass, rabbit and fox with an adult. Direct or build the leaves, caterpillar and robin chain. Point to a wrong arrow, repair it, and show who loses a food source if the plant is covered.
changes.to: Put grass, rabbit and fox in order with an adult. Build the leaves, caterpillar and robin chain too. You can tell an adult where to put each card. Find a wrong arrow and fix it. Cover the plant. Who loses a food source?

changes.from: Build both chains, label producer and consumer, and repair one reversed arrow. Explain how a loss of plants could affect the next two organisms.
changes.to: Build both chains. Add producer and consumer labels. Fix one arrow that points the wrong way. If there are fewer plants, what could change for the next two living things? Say why.

changes.from: Compare both chains and explain an indirect effect of fewer plants. State why a real animal may have other food sources, so the model does not guarantee exactly what a population will do.
changes.to: Compare both chains. If there are fewer plants, what could change for an animal that does not eat plants? Explain the steps. A real animal may eat other foods too. Why can this simple model not tell us the exact number of animals that will live?

changes.from: Recover Monday’s three-link chain. Point along an arrow and say who receives the food.
changes.to: Find Monday’s chain of three. Follow an arrow. Say who gets the food.

changes.from: Build both supplied example chains using paper labels. Make one arrow deliberately wrong and repair it with the feeding clues. Cover the plant in one chain and predict what could change for the next two organisms.
changes.to: Build both chains with the paper labels. Make one arrow point the wrong way. Use the feeding clues to fix it. Cover the plant in one chain. Predict what could change for the next two living things. Say why.

changes.from: Check the arrow direction and one prediction with an adult or chosen partner. Use the feeding clue, not just the order of the names.
changes.to: Check an arrow and one prediction with an adult or a partner. Use the feeding clue. The order of the names alone will not tell us why.

changes.from: Restore or revise the chain, explain one consequence and one model limit, then save a labelled picture and clear the table.
changes.to: Put the chain back or change it. Say one thing that could happen. Say one thing the model cannot tell us. Save a labelled picture. Clear the table.

changes.from: Printed organism labels, arrow strips and a paper cover. No animals or plants are collected or fed. An adult may move every card under the pupil’s direction.
changes.to: Use printed names of living things, arrow strips and a paper cover. Do not collect or feed real plants or animals. You can tell an adult where to move each card.
